articles.title: France and Germany lock horns over long-term EU budget
articles.text:
France and Germany lock horns over long-term EU budget
Advertisement
Politics
France and Germany lock horns over long-term EU budget
AFP - news@thelocal.com
Published: 10 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 10 Oct 2026 15:49 CET
Add a comment
France's President Emmanuel Macron (L) and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (R). Photo by INA FASSBENDER / AFP.
Add The Local as a preferred source
Daggers have been drawn over the European Union's next seven-year budget, with Germany and France at loggerheads over whether Brussels should make deep cuts in a battle increasingly expected to overshoot the end of the year.
The EU wants a deal by Christmas, fearing that any delay would push talks into a fraught election year with worries about what eurosceptic victories in France and elsewhere would mean for future dealmaking.
That is a far from easy task after the European Commission proposed a 2028-2034 budget worth nearly €2 trillion. The 2021-2027 budget was worth around €1.2 trillion.
Europe is deeply divided. Germany leads a pack with Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden, which want cuts of several hundred billion euros.
Advertisement
But France, the second-biggest European economy and a net contributor to the budget, argues the continent needs sufficient means to match the rising challenges the 27-country bloc faces.
French President Emmanuel Macron has hit out at demands for massive cuts.
"We need an ambitious European budget," he said last month. "We must defend a much stronger European budget" to support EU priorities, including defence.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating EU presidency, will unveil a revised budget proposal on Saturday that it hopes will bridge the yawning gap between the sides.
The warnings from European officials are stark, however: it is unavoidable that there will be blood on the floor at the end of the painful negotiations.
But the risk of missing the December deadline now looms larger than ever, especially after Spain called a snap election for next month.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
'Shared sense of urgency'
A senior European diplomat dismissed speculation before Saturday's text.
The EU knows "there is a shared sense of urgency around the need to do this", the diplomat said, adding: "I don't think it's particularly fruitful discussion at this stage to start talking about alternatives."
In absolute terms, the EU does not need to agree the budget this year, as the final legal deadline is the end of 2027.
Saturday's proposal will set the stage for a fist fight between EU leaders meeting in Brussels over two days next week.
The battle won't just be over whether to cut since a third side has its own demands.
Seventeen countries from southern, central and eastern Europe have formed a group known as the "Friends of Cohesion", seeking greater funding to support agriculture and regional development.
The main gripe for the frugals is the proposed budget represents an increase of around 60 percent at a time when member states have to tighten their belts.
But a French presidency official argued money was needed for farmers and to strengthen the European economy to help businesses compete with US and Chinese rivals.
"The super-frugals want sweeping cuts and insist on retaining their rebates, effectively weakening the budget," the official said.
Germany and the five other so-called "frugal" EU members in August lashed out at a high bloc budget at a time of "painful fiscal consolidation" -- with Chancellor Friedrich Merz politically weakened by the electoral rise of the far-right AfD party.
Advertisement
Collecting tax money
France is struggling with its own budget woes -- and far-right leader Marine Le Pen has backed slashing the French contribution to the EU budget as one way to rein in the country's debt.
The answer, according to the European Commission? New sources of revenue, rather than larger contributions from member states.
Brussels has put forward plans for a tax on large companies, a levy on electronic waste, and higher tobacco taxes. The European Parliament wants to go further with taxes on digital giants and online gambling.
It remains to be seen whether Ireland will add more ideas for revenue sources, since many nations dislike the tax on big companies and oppose a digital levy.

articles.title: Banking in France: where should you put your savings?
articles.text:
Banking in France: where should you put your savings?
Presented by bunq
Banking in France: where should you put your savings?
Figuring out where to put your savings as an international resident in France can be tricky. We look at some of the options available to help you decide what works best for you.
Published: Wed 26 Aug 2026 13:49 CEST
Make your savings work for you while you enjoy life abroad. Image by Penny from Pixabay
Moving to France is a dream come true for many, whether you're seeking a slower pace of life at a seaside town in Brittany or café culture in Paris.
But the reality of settling into a new country can be overwhelming. Along with keeping up with carte de séjour renewals, you also have to find an apartment and adapt to local life.
It's no wonder that banking often ends up low on the priority list, especially when opening an account often involves paperwork, appointments and conversations in a language you're still learning.
Yet where you keep your savings can make a huge difference over time. While many residents automatically open le Livret A, France's best-known savings account, it's not the only option available.
For internationals looking to manage their finances in English, digital banks such as bunq offer another way to organise and grow your money.
So how do the different options compare? We break down the key details to help you decide where to put your savings.
Find out how bunq combines everyday banking and saving in one app
The French default: The Livret A
If you've spent any time in France, you've probably heard someone mention the Livret A.
Similar to a cash ISA in the UK, the Livret A is France's most widely used savings account and is available through most banks.
As a regulated savings product, its interest rate is set by the French state, making it a familiar choice for people looking for a straightforward place to keep their savings.
One of its biggest advantages is that the interest you earn is tax-free. Your money also remains accessible, so you can make withdrawals when you need to.
Figuring out the best way to manage your savings in France can be tricky. Image by rawpixel from Pixabay
However, it's worth looking at the full picture. The Livret A interest rate is reviewed regularly, with inflation taken into account. As of August 2026, the rate is 1.7 percent, up from 1.5 percent previously.
There's also a legal deposit limit of €22,950. Once you've reached that amount, you can't make further deposits into the account, although interest can continue to build beyond the limit. So if you have more than €22,950 to save, you need to consider another account.
Another thing to keep in mind is that Livret A is a dedicated savings account. To earn interest, you first have to move money into it, while the cash sitting in your everyday accounts – for things like rent or groceries – doesn't earn Livret A interest.
Meanwhile, to set the account up, customers may have to go in person to a bank.
For many people, the Livret A is a good option. But if you're new to France, prefer to check your finances in English or want to explore alternatives, it's worth knowing what else is available.
Another approach to growing your money
European neobank bunq takes a different approach to saving.
Currently, bunq offers a 3.01 percent gross bonus interest, while its base rate stands at 1.51 percent. Both rates are before tax.
For new savers, the bonus rate applies to all of your savings until your first threshold calculation.
After that, the interest rate depends on your personal threshold, which is calculated using the highest balance held in your Savings Account during the previous six months. The base rate applies to savings up to that threshold, while the bonus rate applies to savings above it.
An element praised by bunq customers is that interest is paid out weekly rather than annually, meaning you don't have to wait until the end of the year to receive it.
Another of bunq's most distinctive features is something it calls MassInterest, which kicks in when you open a bunq Savings Account.
Instead of earning interest only on money you've transferred into your separate Savings Account, balances across your bunq accounts generate interest automatically.
What that means in practice is if you have set aside €1,000 to pay next month's bills, that money will continue earning interest until you spend it, rather than sitting idle in your current account. There's no need to remember to move money into a separate savings pot first.
MassInterest applies to savings of up to €100,000. There is no penalty or negative interest on amounts above €100,000, but amounts above this do not earn MassInterest interest.
Deposits held with bunq are also protected under the Dutch Deposit Guarantee Scheme up to €100,000 per account holder.
What difference could that make?
Imagine you are a new customer who deposits €20,000 in your account and keeps it there over a three-month period. Based on the advertised rates as of August 2026:
With the Livret A, you'd earn around €85 in tax-free interest.
With bunq, you'd receive roughly €106 after tax, based on around €151 in gross interest at the current 3.01 percent bonus rate and weekly compounding. This amount is calculated after France's 30 percent flat tax on investment income (the prélèvement forfaitaire unique, or PFU).
Even after tax, you could earn €21 more with bunq over the same three-month period. Our example is for illustrative purposes and the amount of interest you receive depends on when you open the account.
However, there's another important difference to keep in mind. With the Livret A, only the money you've manually transferred into your Savings Account earns interest. With bunq's MassInterest, eligible balances across your accounts generate interest without you having to do anything.
Download the bunq app and explore its savings options
bunq's app can be set up fully in English. Photo: bunq
Made for international life

articles.title: Inside France: Burning bins and smart slogans at French student protests
articles.text:
Inside France: Burning bins and smart slogans at French student protests
Advertisement
Inside France
Members only
Inside France: Burning bins and smart slogans at French student protests
Emma Pearson - emma.pearson@thelocal.com
Published: 10 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 10 Oct 2026 11:15 CET
Add a comment
A protester holds a placard reading "The revolution begins with our courage" in front of the July Column during a demonstration of high-school students at Place de la Bastille, in Paris, on October 8, 2026, as part of a nationwide protest movement over learning conditions. Photo by Kenzo TRIBOUILLARD / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
From the student protests engulfing France to the vexed issue of police violence - via a brief divergence into why bins always end up on fire - and a vegetarian wolf, here are the latest news and talking points from France.
Inside France is editor Emma Pearson's weekly look at some of the news, talking points and gossip in France that you might not have heard about. It’s published each Saturday and members can receive it directly to their inbox, by going to their newsletter preferences or adding their email to the sign-up box in this article.
News from France this week has been dominated by student protests as hundreds of thousands of teenage pupils at lycées took to the streets to demand more resources for education - a movement that started small but quickly engulfed the country and was widely reported abroad as a 'student revolt'.
In truth, their demands were quite conservative - more teachers, an increase in the maintenance budget, better organisation of the school day - and have been partially successful; the education minister on Thursday announced the deployment of an extra 3,000 teachers to cover classes where the teacher is absent.
Advertisement
It's worth noting that teachers have been staging strikes about this exact issue for years with no progress - the students' tactics seem to have been more effective.
But as the protests went on, the issues covered have widened into more general political struggles while more and more placards have referenced police violence against the protesters, including the teens who have lost teeth, eyes and hands at the hands of the police.
Whatever your views on the protesters, there's no denying that French kids are world-class slogan writers - among the tens of thousands of placards photographed on the protests there have been funny ones, rude ones, cultural references and astute political points.
READ ALSO: Bac to f**k: Understanding French lycées protest signs
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
It's also interesting how many see themselves as the heirs of the student protesters of May 1968 (which at least shows that they are learning some history) - one placard references 'the 6 7 generation re-staging 68' - referring to the viral TikTok '6-7' trend which obviously I, as an old lady, do not understand.
Talking France
We decided to do a special episode of Talking France on the student protests, speaking to some experts to try and answer questions such as: are French lycées really that bad? How did a protest over teacher numbers get this big? Is this linked to the febrile political atmosphere ahead of the 2027 elections? Listen here.
Advertisement
Perspectives
One thing that always happens when there are big protests in France is that the foreign media descends and does its best to portray the whole country as a flaming war zone - meaning that foreigners living here get a barrage of messages from worried relatives overseas asking if they're OK and advising them to stay indoors.
I wrote about this disconnect and was pleased to see that it resonated with many readers - it is always odd to be going about your day perfectly normally while loved ones overseas are convinced that the entire country is in flames.
READ ALSO: OPINION: Relax, mum, France isn't in flames it's just a bin on fire
Some of this, of course, is the natural tendency of journalists to make everything seem as dramatic as possible, but there are increasingly more sinister explanations, as the French radio station RFI showed with their breakdown of social media posts by influencers based in the UK, US, Russia and Israel - many of the pictures they were sharing were either from different protests or taken in a different country (the 'rioting' teens surrounding a car were actually in Times Square in New York).
Advertisement
Will no one think of the bins?
A favourite media trick is to take a photo of a bin on fire and crop it very closely so that it seems like the city is burning - a wide angle will usually show a single bin on fire while in the background people go about their daily business.
Of course it's not ideal that bins get burned, it's annoying for residents, expensive for local councils and requires deployment of the fire service to put them out. And this is not unique to student protests - every time social unrest flares in France you can more or less guarantee that a bin will get it. I remember during the 2023 riots the large wheeled bin for my building disappeared one night - trying to figure out how to request a replacement, I went to the website of the local mairie, expecting the process to be very complicated, only to be greeted with a pop-up that basically said 'has your bin been burned in a riot? Click here'.
But while this is not ideal, it is, at the end of the day, just a bin - it's not a priceless piece of art, and it's not a sentient being. Is protecting the bins from being burned really worth the increasingly violent policing that we are seeing of these protests? Which do we value more highly - our children or our bins?

articles.title: French Word of the Day: Soixante-huitard
articles.text:
French Word of the Day: Soixante-huitard
Advertisement
French Word of the Day
Members only
French Word of the Day: Soixante-huitard
The Local France - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 9 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 10 Oct 2026 09:45 CET
1 comment
Photo: Annie Spratt/Unsplash/ Nicolas Raymond
Add The Local as a preferred source
About one in five people of a certain French generation can be described using this term.
Why do I need to know soixante-huitard?
Because it references a very important part of French history and culture.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
What does it mean?
Soixante-huitard – pronounced swah-sahnt wheat arr (listen here) - literally means sixty-eighter. While its translation might sound a bit like a sports team (like the Forty-niners),  this term in French has an important political and social context behind it.
A soixante-huitard is someone who participated in the famous May 1968 protests in France. With the backdrop of the Prague Spring and the American Civil Rights Movement and anti-war protests, French students and striking workers demanded a more egalitarian world in May 1968.
This period of civil unrest lasted seven weeks and even forced then-President Charles de Gaulle to temporarily flee to West Germany. The events of this time have had a profound effect on French culture and politics.
Around 11 million people - 22 percent of the population at the time - were involved in some way or another, and these days, those people are referred to as un soixante-huitard or une soixante-huitarde (for a woman).
Advertisement
Though the term is typically reserved to refer to those actually involved in the protest movement, it can occasionally be used as a way to describe someone who has held onto the far-left ideas or sentiments from the 1968 movement.
You might be hearing it more than usual at the moment, as some in the current French lycée student protests refer to themselves as the heirs of May 1968. You may even have seen placards saying 'the 6-7 generation remaking 68' (referencing the viral TikTok 6-7 trend popular with the youth of today).
Use it like this
Il a gardé ses convictions d'extrême gauche longtemps après 1968. C'est un vrai soixante-huitard. – He held onto his far-left beliefs long after 1968. He is a true sixty-eighter.
Tu pourrais être surpris que ta tante ait une soixante-huitarde. Ses opinions ont certainement changé avec le temps. Tu ne l'aurais jamais deviné ! – You might be surprised that your aunt participated in May 68. Her opinions have really changed with time, you would never have guessed it.

Soixante-huitard – pronounced swah-sahnt wheat arr (listen here) - literally means sixty-eighter. While its translation might sound a bit like a sports team (like the Forty-niners),  this term in French has an important political and social context behind it.
A soixante-huitard is someone who participated in the famous May 1968 protests in France. With the backdrop of the Prague Spring and the American Civil Rights Movement and anti-war protests, French students and striking workers demanded a more egalitarian world in May 1968.
This period of civil unrest lasted seven weeks and even forced then-President Charles de Gaulle to temporarily flee to West Germany. The events of this time have had a profound effect on French culture and politics.
Around 11 million people - 22 percent of the population at the time - were involved in some way or another, and these days, those people are referred to as un soixante-huitard or une soixante-huitarde (for a woman).
Advertisement
Though the term is typically reserved to refer to those actually involved in the protest movement, it can occasionally be used as a way to describe someone who has held onto the far-left ideas or sentiments from the 1968 movement.
You might be hearing it more than usual at the moment, as some in the current French lycée student protests refer to themselves as the heirs of May 1968. You may even have seen placards saying 'the 6-7 generation remaking 68' (referencing the viral TikTok 6-7 trend popular with the youth of today).
Use it like this
Il a gardé ses convictions d'extrême gauche longtemps après 1968. C'est un vrai soixante-huitard. – He held onto his far-left beliefs long after 1968. He is a true sixty-eighter.
Tu pourrais être surpris que ta tante ait une soixante-huitarde. Ses opinions ont certainement changé avec le temps. Tu ne l'aurais jamais deviné ! – You might be surprised that your aunt participated in May 68. Her opinions have really changed with time, you would never have guessed it.

Talking France is back with a special episode on the lycée student protests gripping the country - what are the students protesting about, and are their demands reasonable? Why did violence flare? And will this escalate into something much bigger?
Host Ben McPartland is joined by The Local France's Emma Pearson and Emma Albright, politics expert John Lichfield and education expert Peter Gumbel to talk about the student protests that are sweeping France.
You can find the Talking France podcast on Spotify, Apple or the French platform  Deezer or on  World Radio Paris. You can download it  here or listen to the full episode on the link below.
Listeners can join The Local for just €29.99/year. For more info click here.
So what are these protests all about? We trace the beginning of the movement and how it grew into a nationwide issue and ask what the high school (lycée) students actually want.
Stay informed with our essential Talking France newsletter
Next we talk to education expert Peter Gumbel about the problems in French lycées - are they really as bad as the students claim? Are their demands reasonable? And will the government be willing or able to give them what they want?
As the protests have spread over the past week, they have become about more than just teacher shortages and crumbling classrooms, with some predicting that they will become 'the next May 1968'.
We ask John Lichfield how the protests got so big and whether they will continue to grow.
As violence flared, police responded with tear gas, rubber bullets and stun grenades with several teenagers sustaining serious injuries. We discuss the long-standing issue of police violence in France, and whether the heavy-handed response actually fuelled further protests.

Finally we take a look at some of the French vocabulary used during the demos, including deciphering some of the many witty signs that students have taken to their protests.

articles.title: OPINION: French high school student protests are a sign of a country in crisis
articles.text:
OPINION: French high school student protests are a sign of a country in crisis
Advertisement
Politics
Members only
OPINION: French high school student protests are a sign of a country in crisis
John Lichfield - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 5 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 10 Oct 2026 08:23 CET
4 comments
Students blockading the Gustave Eiffel high school in Bordeaux, south-western France on October 5, 2026. Photo by Christophe ARCHAMBAULT / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
How did a protest at a single French high school over a lack of teaching staff escalate so fast into nationwide, sometimes violent, protests? John Lichfield argues that the lycée protests are just a symptom of a country in deep trouble.
This is a dangerous week for France.
I said three weeks ago that the country is in trouble. I was wrong. It is in deep trouble.
Crises are piling on crises. There is a risk that the country will enter a kind of vicious circle or uncontrollable spiral.
The lycée protests will merge on Tuesday with marches by public sector workers who are complaining about government cuts and low wages. The demonstration will attract the usual fringe of trouble-makers from the anarchist ultra-left.
READ ALSO: Strikes and demos: What to expect from Tuesday's 'act 3' of student protests in France
The lycée revolt was, in its origins, a justified protest against large classes, crumbling schools and teacher shortages. It has been infiltrated, and in some cases overwhelmed, by Far Left activists and disaffected teenagers from the inner suburbs of French cities who have more interest in setting fires and stoning the police than education.
READ ALSO: Explained: What are French students protesting about?
On October 17th, the lycée protesters may join the nationwide demonstration and blockages planned to complain about high fuel pump prices. The ghosts of the Gilets Jaunes are being invoked. More violence is inevitable.
Advertisement
The financial markets will observe the mayhem and may conclude that France is becoming socially unstable as well as politically deadlocked. France’s €3.5 trillion accumulated debt was once held mostly by calm, long-term investors. It is increasingly being bought up by hedge-funds whose business model is speculation. They love the smell of a crisis.
If they force up France’s borrowing costs - as they already are - there will be even less public money for agreeing compromise budgets, fixing schools, subsidising fuel prices or increasing civil servants’ wages.
And so the vicious spiral will continue.
A budget war (yet another) is already brewing in the National Assembly against the background of next spring’s presidential election. The bond markets will observe closely a speech on Tuesday by the presidential front-runner, the Far Right leader Marine Le Pen, in which she will list ideas for slashing €250 billion from public spending over five years. She is likely to rehash her previous, incoherent plans to take most of that money from the EU, immigrants and tax fraudsters.
Le Pen will doubtless benefit from the school blockages and street violence. Will she also be damaged by the scandal about the anti-semitic remarks made as a teenager by her Number Two Jordan Bardella? Maybe, a little.
Don't miss John Lichfield's expert French politics analysis
In 30 years in France, I cannot remember a time with so many interlocking crises. What can be done? Not much. Not easily. The problems are long in the making and will be painful in the solving - if they can be solved at all.
The government was slow to react to the original lycée protests in the north-west Paris suburbs three weeks ago. They have now spread to almost a third of the 3,500 lycées in the country, from the multi-racial banlieues to rural towns.
The extreme violence, including the burning of 24 school buildings and 70 attacks on teachers, is inexcusable. It seems mostly to come from intruders, ranging from far-left activists to criminal teenage gangs which love any opportunity to attack the police.
Sending in the police to break up some of the original protests last month was a mistake. The French police are hopeless at crowd control. Crowds – even teenage crowds – love to provoke them. The police love to be provoked.
READ ALSO: France teen protester has hand blown off by police grenade
All the same, it is an unfortunate fact that without the violence we would not be talking about the lycée students’ grievances. Street violence is part of French politics. The scenes in recent days, partly encouraged by Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s Far Left, are a foretaste of what will happen if Le Pen is elected President on May 2nd.
Advertisement
And yet the spread of the protests in the last week cannot all be blamed on political manipulation and the contagion of social media. It suggests that high school student anger and anxiety is widespread and real. Why?
France is one of the highest spending states in the world. It supposedly invests more than the OECD average on public education - over €90 billion a year. Why then are classes overcrowded? Why is there a shortage of replacement teachers? Why are school buildings crumbling and unbearable in a heatwave? Why are teachers underpaid?
READ ALSO: Analysis: Why do French schools do so badly in international rankings?
One could ask the same sort of questions about the French state health service.
The trades unions and the Left blame the alleged cuts of the Macron years. Some mistakes have been made by successive Macron-era governments but health and education have, in theory, been shielded from budget constraints.
And yet many lycées have classes of 35 or more, endemic teacher shortages and decrepit buildings. Where is all the money going?
Advertisement
Here is a seldom spoken truth. Over one quarter of all the money spent on education in France goes on paying the pensions of retired teachers.
Those ex-teachers have earned their pensions. The problem is a system in which the active supposedly pay the pension
